import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjectures in Complexity Theory

This file contains formal statements of some of the main open conjectures
in complexity theory, including

- the P vs NP problem
- the NP vs coNP problem

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_versus_NP_problem)
- [The Clay Institute](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/)
-/

namespace ComplexityTheory

/--
**P ≠ NP**:

The conjecture that the complexity classes P and NP are not equal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 68]
theorem P_ne_NP : P ≠ NP := by sorry

/--
**NP ≠ coNP**:

The conjecture that the complexity classes NP and coNP are not equal.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 68]
theorem NP_ne_coNP : NP ≠ coNP := by sorry

/--
The theorem that the set of complements of languages in P is itself P.

This can be proven by observing that the boolean negation function is computable in polynomial time,
and that compositions of poly-time computable functions are also poly-time computable.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 68]
theorem coP_eq_P :
    { L | Lᶜ ∈ P } = P := by
  sorry

/--
The theorem that P is a subset of NP.

This can be proven by observing that for any language in P,
we can construct a verifier that ignores the witness and simply runs the poly-time decider for the
language.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 68]
theorem P_subset_NP :
    P ⊆ NP := by
  sorry

/--
The theorem that P is a subset of coNP.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 68]
theorem P_subset_coNP :
    P ⊆ coNP := by
  rw [coNP, ← coP_eq_P]
  simp only [Set.ofPred_subset_ofPred]
  intros L hL
  exact P_subset_NP hL

end ComplexityTheory

reformulations.difference: The shared class definitions use Boolean characteristic functions of binary languages, canonical bitstring encodings, and Mathlib's finite-state stack-machine model rather than Cook's presentation using languages over arbitrary finite alphabets and conventional Turing machines.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Cook explicitly permits reduction to a binary alphabet. Boolean characteristic functions correspond bijectively to binary languages. The actual input encoding has length 3|x|, and the pair encoding has length 6|x|+1+3|w|; encoding, decoding, and validation have linear-time implementations. The stack model and conventional Turing machines simulate one another with polynomial overhead, including the required cleanup at termination. Although FinTM2 explicitly requires finiteness only of the input alphabet, finitely many program push sites each map a finite internal-state type into a stack alphabet, so only finitely many symbols are reachable. This does not introduce an infinite-alphabet oracle. Thus these modelling choices preserve the classes used by both separation conjectures.

reformulations.difference: The imported NP definition allows witnesses of length at most p(|x|), with p : Polynomial ℕ. Arora–Barak Definition 2.1 uses witnesses of exactly polynomial length, while Cook uses a power bound |x|^k.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Bounded-length witnesses can be encoded self-delimitingly and padded to an exact polynomial length; the verifier recovers the witness and checks the original bound. Conversely, a bounded-witness verifier can enforce exact length when simulating an exact-length definition. Polynomial bounds can be enlarged and normalized to power bounds while retaining a guard for the original bound, with finitely many short inputs handled directly. These transformations preserve polynomial-time verification. In particular, p = 0 legitimately leaves the empty witness and supports P ⊆ NP; it does not make the witness domain empty.

reformulations.difference: The Lean set is the inverse image {L | Lᶜ ∈ P}, whereas the source describes the set of complements of P languages or closure of P under complementation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Complementation is an involution: Lᶜᶜ = L. Consequently {L | Lᶜ ∈ C} equals the image of C under complementation, and its equality with C is equivalent to ∀ L ∈ C, Lᶜ ∈ C. Both identities were proved generically in the scratch file, along with agreement between pointwise Boolean negation and language complement.
